extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, patent examiners, litigators, inventors, and other practitioners working with U.S. patent infringement/remedies law
extracted.subtask_description: Statutory standards from the U.S. Code (selected sections) defining acts of infringement, defenses, remedies, notice/marking rules, and special exceptions (e.g., regulatory submissions, prior commercial use, medical practitioners).

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint owners' rights
rubrics_metrics.description: In the absence of any agreement to the contrary, each joint owner of a patent may make, use, offer to sell, or sell the patented invention within the United States, or import the patented invention into the United States, without the consent of and without accounting to the other owners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original statutory text (no consent/accounting required among joint owners unless an agreement provides otherwise).

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension of time for government applications (35 U.S.C. 267)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director may extend the time for taking any action to three years when an application has become property of the United States and the head of the appropriate department certifies the invention is important to armament or defense of the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural standard for timing when government acquires application; statutory conditions for Director's extension authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of infringement (35 U.S.C. 271(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Except as otherwise provided, whoever without authority makes, uses, offers to sell, or sells any patented invention within the United States, or imports into the United States any patented invention during the term of the patent, infringes the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Core act-of-infringement definition; applies during the patent term unless statute provides exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active inducement liability (35 U.S.C. 271(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Whoever actively induces infringement of a patent shall be liable as an infringer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate basis of liability from direct infringement; requires proof of inducement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contributory infringement (35 U.S.C. 271(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Whoever offers to sell or sells within the United States or imports into the United States a component of a patented machine, manufacture, combination, or composition, or a material or apparatus for use in practicing a patented process, constituting a material part of the invention, knowing the same to be especially made or especially adapted for use in an infringement of such patent, and not a staple article or commodity of commerce suitable for substantial noninfringing use, shall be liable as a contributory infringer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elements: (1) component/material is a material part; (2) knowledge it is specially made/adapted for infringement; (3) not a staple article suitable for substantial noninfringing use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on misuse/denial of relief (35 U.S.C. 271(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: No patent owner otherwise entitled to relief shall be denied relief or deemed guilty of misuse or illegal extension of the patent right by reason of having done certain acts (e.g., derived revenue from acts that would be contributory infringement if done by another, licensed or authorized others, sought to enforce rights, refused to license or use rights, or conditioned licenses/sales) unless the patent owner has market power in the relevant market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists specific conduct that does not constitute misuse per se; market power exception limits the safe harbor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory-submission safe harbor (35 U.S.C. 271(e)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not an act of infringement to make, use, offer to sell, or sell within the United States or import a patented invention solely for uses reasonably related to the development and submission of information under a Federal law regulating the manufacture, use, or sale of drugs or veterinary biological products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Safe harbor for activities related to regulatory approval (Hatch‑Waxman style); excludes certain new animal drugs/veterinary biological products primarily manufactured using specified biotechnologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acts treated as infringement for submitting certain drug/biologic applications (35 U.S.C. 271(e)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: It shall be an act of infringement to submit specified applications under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (e.g., section 505(j), certain 505(b)(2) applications, section 512, or March 4, 1913 Act) for a drug or veterinary biological product claimed in a patent or whose use is claimed in a patent, subject to statutory definitions and exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines when filing certain regulatory applications can constitute an act of infringement for purposes of remedies and litigation involving pharmaceuticals/biologics.

rubrics_metrics.name: No injunctive relief for activities permitted under (e)(1) (35 U.S.C. 271(e)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: In any action for patent infringement under this section, no injunctive or other relief may be granted which would prohibit the making, using, offering to sell, or selling within the United States or importing into the United States of a patented invention under paragraph (1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may not enjoin regulatory‑submission activities protected by the safe harbor; remedies are limited accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies and special rules for drug/biologic-related infringement (35 U.S.C. 271(e)(4) and related)
rubrics_metrics.description: For infringement arising from submissions described in paragraph (2), the statute prescribes remedies and limitations: e.g., court shall order effective date of approval not earlier than patent expiration; injunctive relief may be available against infringer to prevent commercial manufacture/use of an approved drug or biological product; for certain biological products the sole and exclusive remedy may be a reasonable royalty; damages only if there has been commercial manufacture/use/sale/importation of an approved product; permanent injunctions may be ordered until patent expiration under specified conditions; attorney fees may still be awarded under section 285.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex scheme distinguishing drugs, veterinary biologics, and biological products; contains time/notice conditions and conditions for exclusive remedies versus injunctive relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liability for supplying components from the U.S. for foreign combination (35 U.S.C. 271(f)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: Whoever without authority supplies or causes to be supplied in or from the United States all or a substantial portion of the components of a patented invention, where such components are uncombined in whole or in part, in such manner as to actively induce the combination of such components outside of the United States in a manner that would infringe the patent if such combination occurred within the United States, shall be liable as an infringer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Targets supply from U.S. that actively induces infringing combinations abroad; focuses on substantial portion of components and active inducement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liability for supplying especially made/adapted components for foreign combination (35 U.S.C. 271(f)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Whoever supplies or causes to be supplied in or from the United States any component of a patented invention that is especially made or especially adapted for use in the invention and not a staple article suitable for substantial noninfringing use, uncombined and knowing it is so made or adapted and intending that it will be combined outside the United States in a manner that would infringe if combined within the U.S., shall be liable as an infringer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Addresses specially made components exported uncombined with knowledge and intent for infringement once combined abroad.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement by importation of product made by patented process (35 U.S.C. 271(g))
rubrics_metrics.description: Whoever without authority imports into the United States or offers to sell, sells, or uses within the United States a product which is made by a process patented in the United States shall be liable as an infringer, if the importation, offer to sell, sale, or use occurs during the term of such process patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides remedy against importing products made by a patented process; exceptions if the product is materially changed by subsequent processes or becomes a trivial/nonessential component of another product.

rubrics_metrics.name: States subject to patent law (35 U.S.C. 271(h))
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'whoever' includes any State, instrumentality of a State, any officer or employee of a State acting in official capacity; any State and such entities shall be subject to the provisions of this title in the same manner and extent as nongovernmental entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies that state actors can be liable under patent statutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'offer for sale' (35 U.S.C. 271(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'offer for sale' or an 'offer to sell' by a person other than the patentee or any assignee of the patentee is that in which the sale will occur before the expiration of the term of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies timing-based definition of offers for sale by third parties relative to patent term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporary presence defense (35 U.S.C. 272)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of any invention in any vessel, aircraft, or vehicle of any country entering the United States temporarily or accidentally, where that country affords similar privileges to U.S. vessels, shall not constitute infringement if the invention is used exclusively for the needs of the vessel/aircraft/vehicle and is not offered for sale or sold in or used for manufacture of anything to be sold in or exported from the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limited exemption for temporary/accidental presence of foreign vessels/aircraft/vehicles and exclusive use for their needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior commercial use defense (35 U.S.C. 273(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: A person shall be entitled to a defense under section 282(b) with respect to subject matter consisting of a process or machine/manufacture/composition used in a manufacturing or other commercial process that would otherwise infringe, if such person, acting in good faith, commercially used the subject matter in the United States (internal commercial use or arm's length sale/transfer of a useful end result) and such commercial use occurred at least 1 year before the earlier of (A) the effective filing date of the claimed invention or (B) the date the invention was publicly disclosed qualifying for the exception under section 102(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishes elements of the prior commercial use defense: good faith, commercial use in the U.S., and timing at least one year before filing or qualifying disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof for prior commercial use (35 U.S.C. 273(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: A person asserting a defense under this section shall have the burden of establishing the defense by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher evidentiary standard for asserting this defense in litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Premarketing regulatory review deemed commercial use (35 U.S.C. 273(c)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject matter for which commercial marketing or use is subject to a premarketing regulatory review period during which safety or efficacy is established shall be deemed to be commercially used for purposes of subsection (a)(1) during such regulatory review period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treats time in regulatory review as commercial use for prior commercial use defense purposes (including periods specified in section 156(g)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonprofit laboratory use treated as commercial use (35 U.S.C. 273(c)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: A use by a nonprofit research laboratory or other nonprofit entity (e.g., university or hospital) for which the public is the intended beneficiary shall be deemed a commercial use for purposes of subsection (a)(1), except the defense may be asserted only for continued and noncommercial use by and in the laboratory or nonprofit entity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrows applicability: nonprofit uses can qualify, but remedy/defense limited to continued noncommercial use within the nonprofit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhaustion by sale or disposition (35 U.S.C. 273(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: The sale or other disposition of a useful end result by a person entitled to assert a defense under this section shall exhaust the patent owner's rights under the patent to the extent equivalent to exhaustion had the sale been made by the patent owner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishes exhaustion principle for end results sold by a person with a valid prior-use defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on who may assert prior commercial use (personal defense and transfer restrictions) (35 U.S.C. 273(e)(1)-(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: Defense may be asserted only by the person who performed or directed the commercial use, or by an entity that controls/is controlled by/under common control with such person; the right to assert the defense is not licensable or assignable except as an ancillary/subordinate part of a good-faith assignment or transfer of the entire enterprise or line of business; defense when acquired by assignment may only be asserted for uses at sites where subject matter was in use before the later of the effective filing date or date of assignment/transfer. Also, defense is not a general license but extends only to the specific subject matter established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines personal nature of the defense, restrictions on assignment/licensing, site-limited scope, and that it is not a blanket license under all patent claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivation disqualifies prior commercial use defense (35 U.S.C. 273(e)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: A person may not assert the defense if the subject matter on which the defense is based was derived from the patentee or persons in privity with the patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevents asserting prior use based on information derived from the patentee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandonment of commercial use bars reliance on prior activities (35 U.S.C. 273(e)(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who has abandoned commercial use of subject matter may not rely on activities performed before the date of such abandonment in establishing a defense with respect to actions taken on or after the date of abandonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires continuous commercial use; abandonment severs the defense for subsequent acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: University exception to prior commercial use defense (35 U.S.C. 273(e)(5))
rubrics_metrics.description: A person commercially using subject matter may not assert the defense if the claimed invention was, at the time made, owned or subject to an obligation of assignment to an institution of higher education or to a technology transfer organization whose primary purpose is commercialization of technologies developed by such institutions, except when activities required to reduce the invention to practice could not have been undertaken using funds provided by the Federal Government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limits defense for inventions tied to universities/technology transfer organizations, with narrow exception tied to federal funding constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unreasonable assertion of defense leads to exceptional-case finding (35 U.S.C. 273(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: If the defense is pleaded by a person who is found to infringe and who subsequently fails to demonstrate a reasonable basis for asserting the defense, the court shall find the case exceptional for the purpose of awarding attorney fees under section 285.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discourages frivolous or baseless assertions of the prior commercial use defense by making failure to show reasonable basis a ground for attorney-fee shifting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assertion of prior use defense does not render patent invalid (35 U.S.C. 273(g))
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent shall not be deemed to be invalid under sections 102 or 103 solely because a defense is raised or established under this section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishes that prior use defense is distinct from invalidity grounds; asserting or proving it does not invalidate the patent per se.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentee's remedy by civil action (35 U.S.C. 281)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee shall have remedy by civil action for infringement of his patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statement of availability of civil suit to enforce patent rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of validity and enumerated defenses (35 U.S.C. 282)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent shall be presumed valid; each claim is presumed valid independently; burden of establishing invalidity rests on the party asserting it. Defenses that shall be pleaded include noninfringement, absence of liability, unenforceability, invalidity on any ground specified in Part II (conditions for patentability), failure to comply with section 112 (except failure to disclose best mode is not a basis to cancel/hold invalid), failure to comply with section 251, and any other fact or act made a defense by this title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets pleading obligations and preserves claim-by-claim presumption; explicitly limits best-mode challenge and enumerates permissible defenses and pleading requirements (including notice-of-actions requirements described in subsection (c)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice-of-actions and required pretrial disclosures (35 U.S.C. 282(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: In actions involving validity or infringement, the party asserting invalidity or noninfringement shall give notice in the pleadings or otherwise in writing at least thirty days before trial of patents, publications, or persons relied upon as prior inventor/knowledge/uses/offers for sale. In absence of such notice, proof of those matters may not be made at trial except on terms ordered by the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural requirement to provide pretrial notice of prior art or prior use relied upon to contest validity or noninfringement; also provides that invalidity of patent-term extension for failure to comply with section 154(b) or 156 can be pleaded as a defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable injunctions for patent violations (35 U.S.C. 283)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts having jurisdiction may grant injunctions in accordance with principles of equity to prevent violation of any right secured by patent, on such terms as the court deems reasonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard equitable injunction authority; courts apply equity principles in patent cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages award standard (35 U.S.C. 284)
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon finding for the claimant the court shall award damages adequate to compensate for the infringement but in no event less than a reasonable royalty, together with interest and costs. The court may increase damages up to three times the amount found or assessed; increased damages do not apply to provisional rights under section 154(d). The court may receive expert testimony as an aid to determination of damages or reasonable royalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishes compensatory damages floor (reasonable royalty), discretionary treble damages for enhancement, and allowance for expert evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attorney fees in exceptional cases (35 U.S.C. 285)
rubrics_metrics.description: The court in exceptional cases may award reasonable attorney fees to the prevailing party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard for fee shifting; cross-references exceptional-case findings (e.g., baseless defenses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Time limitation on damages (35 U.S.C. 286)
rubrics_metrics.description: Except as otherwise provided by law, no recovery shall be had for any infringement committed more than six years prior to the filing of the complaint or counterclaim for infringement. Special rules apply for claims against the U.S. Government where a pre-suit period may not be counted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statute of limitations for monetary recovery limited to six years preceding filing; provides carve-outs for governmental claims and administrative claim periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marking and notice to recover damages (35 U.S.C. 287(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentees and persons making, offering for sale, selling, or importing patented articles may give notice to the public that the same is patented by fixing on them the word 'patent' or 'pat.' together with the patent number, or by using a publicly accessible Internet address associating the article with the patent number, or by labeling the package. Failure to so mark bars recovery of damages except on proof that the infringer was notified of the infringement and continued to infringe, in which event damages may be recovered only for infringement after such notice; filing an action constitutes such notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marking preserves the patentee's ability to recover pre-suit damages; alternative virtual marking by internet address permitted; filing suit constitutes notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special remedies and good-faith disclosure requests for 271(g) importation claims (35 U.S.C. 287(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: An infringer under section 271(g) shall be subject to damages and injunctions except as modified by this subsection: no remedies are available for a product in the possession of or in transit to the person liable before that person had notice; in determining remedies courts shall consider defendant's good faith with respect to a request for disclosure (a written request made before first importation/use/sale and before notice), responses to such requests, and need to restore exclusive rights. Evidence of good faith includes making a request, reasonable response time, and submission of response to manufacturer/supplier with request for written statement the process is not used. Failure to perform these acts is evidence of absence of good faith unless mitigating circumstances exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a safe-harbor-like procedure for importers to request disclosure of process patents from manufacturers/suppliers and makes cooperative conduct evidence of good faith affecting remedies for 271(g) cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and limits of 'request for disclosure' and attendant fee (35 U.S.C. 287(b)(4)-(6))
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'request for disclosure' is a written request to a manufacturer to identify all process patents owned or licensed that the requester reasonably believes could be asserted under 271(g) if the product were imported/sold/used in the U.S.; limited to requesters regularly engaged in the sale of such products or showing plans to engage in such sales; response obligations, evidence of notice, and a fee (reasonable actual costs not to exceed cost of automated search, but in no case more than $500) apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines who may make requests, what must be included, response obligations, and caps on fees for compliance with disclosure requests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice of infringement definitions and effects (35 U.S.C. 287(b)(5))
rubrics_metrics.description: Notice of infringement means actual knowledge or receipt of written notification or combination thereof of information sufficient to persuade a reasonable person that it is likely a product was made by a patented process. A written notification must specify the patented process alleged and reasons for a good faith belief; recipient who transmits the notification to the manufacturer/supplier and receives a written statement from them setting forth a well-grounded factual basis that patents are not infringed will be deemed not to have notice absent mitigating circumstances. Abnormally large purchases may be rebuttably presumed to give actual knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Details content of written notifications, transmission obligations, what constitutes notice, and presumptions for abnormal purchase quantities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fee for responding to request for disclosure (35 U.S.C. 287(b)(6))
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who receives a response to a request for disclosure shall pay a reasonable fee to cover actual costs, not exceeding the cost of a commercially available automated patent search, and in no case more than $500.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caps the cost recoverable for complying with disclosure requests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medical practitioner exemption from certain remedies (35 U.S.C. 287(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: With respect to a medical practitioner's performance of a medical activity that constitutes infringement under section 271(a) or (b), the provisions of sections 281, 283, 284, and 285 shall not apply against the medical practitioner or against a related health care entity with respect to such medical activity, subject to definitions and exceptions (e.g., does not include use of patented machine or practice of a patented use of a composition that directly contributes to the objective, and does not apply to commercial development/manufacture/sale/import/distribution activities or certain regulated activities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides limited immunity for medical/surgical procedures by licensed practitioners (and related entities) but carves out uses involving patented machines/compositions or commercial activities and certain regulated functions; contains detailed definitions (medical activity, medical practitioner, related health care entity, professional affiliation, body).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability date exclusions (various)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain subsections/statutory provisions specify applicability limits by filing date or effective date (e.g., subsection (c) of 287 does not apply to patents issued based on an application with an effective filing date before Sept. 30, 1996; editorial notes regarding AIA applicability to section 288), and amendments with effective dates are noted throughout.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple provisions in the statute set temporal limits or applicability depending on filing/issue dates or AIA transition rules; practitioners must check effective-date language when applying rules.
